summary:
The Martian Survival Atlas is our solution to the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map.” It is a layered map that combines data from five NASA Mars missions (MRO, Mars Global Surveyor, Mars Odyssey, Curiosity and Perseverance) to help astronauts plan safe, science-rich Marswalks.

The Atlas merges 12 data layers, including terrain, ground firmness, minerals, radiation and weather, and turns them into clear decisions. Its Lifeline engine always knows the way home, using an Apollo-inspired rule: turn back when life support reaches 1.2 × walk-back time + 30 minutes. It plans routes that avoid steep slopes and soft sand. It also ranks science stops by value per minute and gives a GO / CAUTION / NO-GO verdict with clear reasons. A survival mode handles emergencies like dust storms and suit problems, and everything works offline because of the 3–22 minute signal delay to Earth.
details:
What it does: The Martian Survival Atlas is a layered map that helps astronauts plan safe, science-rich Marswalks. It combines 12 data layers from five NASA Mars missions, covering terrain, minerals, radiation, weather and ice. Four engines turn this data into decisions:

  • A Lifeline that always knows the way home, using an Apollo-inspired turn-back rule.
  • Route planning that avoids steep slopes and soft sand.
  • A science-per-minute score that ranks the best stops.
  • A GO / CAUTION / NO-GO verdict with clear reasons.

Benefits and impact: Safer walks, better science and full offline use despite the 3–22 minute delay to Earth. The engine could also support Artemis moonwalks and help students explore real NASA data.

Tools: NASA PDS, USGS, Mars Trek and MMGIS data. The planned prototype uses Python, A* routing and TypeScript with MapLibre/CesiumJS. The deck was designed in Canva, and AI tools (Claude) assisted with research and writing.

Creativity: It plans the way home first, turning Apollo’s walkback limit into a live safety tool. It also adds a science-per-minute score and a digital wrist checklist.

Factors considered: Safety limits from Apollo and NASA research, honest labeling of data quality and limits, and testing against Perseverance’s real route at Jezero Crater.
